name: Tricuspid Valve
summary: The right atrioventricular valve. Its three leaflets, chordae tendineae and papillary muscles prevent regurgitation into the right atrium during ventricular systole.

anatomy.location: At the right atrioventricular junction, set slightly more apically than the mitral valve — an offset that identifies the morphological right ventricle and is exaggerated in Ebstein's anomaly.
anatomy.shape: Three leaflets — anterior (usually largest), posterior and septal — attached to a saddle-shaped, non-planar annulus. The largest of the four valve orifices.
relations: Inferiorly: the right ventricular cavity and its papillary muscles
Medially: the membranous interventricular septum and, immediately adjacent, the AV node and bundle of His
The triangle of Koch, bounded by the septal leaflet, the tendon of Todaro and the coronary sinus ostium, contains the AV node
attachments: Tricuspid annulus, part of the fibrous skeleton
Chordae tendineae from anterior, posterior and septal papillary muscles
Septal leaflet chordae attaching directly to the interventricular septum
anatomy.bloodSupply: Right coronary artery; the valve leaflets themselves are largely avascular and nourished by diffusion.
anatomy.venousDrainage: Small cardiac vein territory, draining to the coronary sinus.
anatomy.innervation: Cardiac plexus fibres reach the annulus and subvalvular apparatus; leaflet tissue is minimally innervated.
anatomy.function: Opens passively in diastole when right atrial pressure exceeds right ventricular pressure, and closes at the onset of systole when that gradient reverses.

physiology.function: Enforces unidirectional flow from right atrium to right ventricle. Competent closure depends on the whole apparatus — annulus, leaflets, chordae, papillary muscles and the ventricular wall that anchors them.

pressures.label: Opening
pressures.value: when RA pressure exceeds RV pressure in early diastole

pressures.label: Closure
pressures.value: at the onset of right ventricular systole

pressures.label: Orifice area
pressures.value: approximately 4–6 cm², the largest cardiac valve

physiology.electrical: Not electrically active itself, but the AV node and penetrating bundle lie immediately adjacent to the septal leaflet, which is why tricuspid annular surgery and ablation risk heart block.
hemodynamics: Contributes to the first heart sound, closing marginally after the mitral valve
Tricuspid regurgitant velocity is used to estimate pulmonary artery systolic pressure by echocardiography
Right-sided murmurs characteristically increase with inspiration — Carvallo's sign
Annular dilatation from right ventricular enlargement is the commonest cause of tricuspid regurgitation

pathology.name: Tricuspid regurgitation
pathology.note: Most often secondary (functional), caused by annular dilatation and right ventricular remodelling rather than primary leaflet disease.

pathology.name: Infective endocarditis
pathology.note: The right-sided valve most often involved, particularly in injection drug use and with intracardiac devices.

pathology.name: Ebstein's anomaly
pathology.note: Congenital apical displacement of the septal and posterior leaflets, atrialising part of the right ventricle.

pathology.name: Rheumatic tricuspid disease
pathology.note: Uncommon in isolation; usually accompanies rheumatic mitral disease.

clinical.relevance: Long regarded as the 'forgotten valve', tricuspid regurgitation is now recognised as an independent predictor of poor outcome, and transcatheter repair and replacement are a rapidly developing field.
examination: Pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal edge increasing on inspiration
Giant v waves in the jugular venous pulse
Peripheral oedema and ascites in severe chronic regurgitation
imaging: Transthoracic echocardiography for leaflet morphology, annular diameter and regurgitation severity
Three-dimensional echocardiography for the non-planar annulus
Cardiac MRI for right ventricular volumes and regurgitant fraction
procedures: Surgical annuloplasty, commonly performed at the time of left-sided valve surgery
Transcatheter edge-to-edge repair and transcatheter tricuspid valve replacement
Careful lead management, since pacing leads crossing the valve can cause regurgitation

keyPoints: Three leaflets — anterior, posterior and septal — and the largest valve orifice in the heart.
Sits slightly more apically than the mitral valve; this offset defines the morphological right ventricle.
The AV node lies in the triangle of Koch adjacent to the septal leaflet — a surgical and ablation hazard.
Most tricuspid regurgitation is functional, driven by annular dilatation.
Right-sided murmurs increase on inspiration (Carvallo's sign).

name: Mitral Valve
summary: The left atrioventricular valve. Two leaflets, a saddle-shaped annulus, chordae tendineae and two papillary muscles keep flow moving from left atrium to left ventricle only.

anatomy.location: At the left atrioventricular junction, positioned slightly more basally than the tricuspid valve.
anatomy.shape: Two leaflets: a large, deep anterior (aortic) leaflet occupying about one third of the annular circumference, and a shallower posterior (mural) leaflet divided into three scallops conventionally labelled P1, P2 and P3, with corresponding anterior segments A1–A3. The annulus is saddle-shaped rather than planar.
relations: Inferiorly: the left ventricular cavity and its papillary muscles
Anteriorly: fibrous continuity with the non-coronary and left coronary cusps of the aortic valve — the aortomitral curtain
The left circumflex artery and coronary sinus run close to the posterior annulus
attachments: Mitral annulus, a component of the cardiac fibrous skeleton
Chordae tendineae from the anterolateral and posteromedial papillary muscles — each papillary muscle sends chordae to both leaflets
anatomy.bloodSupply: Anterolateral papillary muscle has dual supply from the left anterior descending and left circumflex arteries; the posteromedial papillary muscle usually has a single supply from the posterior descending artery, making it far more vulnerable to ischaemic rupture.
anatomy.venousDrainage: Great cardiac vein and coronary sinus territory.
anatomy.innervation: Cardiac plexus fibres to the annulus and subvalvular apparatus.
anatomy.function: Opens when left atrial pressure exceeds left ventricular pressure and closes at the onset of ventricular systole; leaflet coaptation depends on coordinated function of every component of the apparatus.

physiology.function: Permits low-resistance ventricular filling in diastole and seals the left ventricle during systole so that the full stroke volume is directed to the aorta.

pressures.label: Opening
pressures.value: when LA pressure exceeds LV pressure in early diastole

pressures.label: Closure
pressures.value: at the onset of left ventricular systole, generating the first heart sound

pressures.label: Severe stenosis
pressures.value: orifice area of about 1.5 cm² or less

physiology.electrical: Not electrically active. Mitral annular disjunction and mitral valve prolapse have been associated with ventricular arrhythmia in a minority of patients.
hemodynamics: Mitral closure produces the dominant component of the first heart sound
In stenosis, the transmitral gradient rises steeply with heart rate because diastolic filling time shortens
In regurgitation, part of the stroke volume is ejected backwards into the left atrium, so total stroke volume rises while forward output falls
Systolic anterior motion of the anterior leaflet contributes to outflow obstruction in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy

pathology.name: Mitral regurgitation
pathology.note: Primary (degenerative, prolapse, chordal rupture) or secondary (annular dilatation and leaflet tethering from ventricular remodelling).

pathology.name: Mitral stenosis
pathology.note: Overwhelmingly rheumatic in origin worldwide, with commissural fusion and leaflet thickening.

pathology.name: Mitral valve prolapse
pathology.note: Myxomatous leaflet degeneration with billowing into the left atrium; the commonest cause of primary mitral regurgitation in high-income settings.

pathology.name: Papillary muscle rupture
pathology.note: A mechanical complication of myocardial infarction producing acute, severe mitral regurgitation and cardiogenic shock.

pathology.name: Infective endocarditis
pathology.note: Vegetations may cause leaflet perforation or chordal rupture with acute regurgitation.

clinical.relevance: The mitral valve is the most common target of structural heart intervention after the aortic valve, and its assessment — leaflet segment, mechanism and severity — directly determines whether repair, replacement or transcatheter therapy is appropriate.
examination: Pansystolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla in regurgitation
Mid-diastolic rumble with an opening snap and loud first heart sound in stenosis
Mid-systolic click with a late systolic murmur in prolapse
Malar flush and atrial fibrillation in longstanding rheumatic stenosis
imaging: Transthoracic echocardiography for mechanism and severity
Transoesophageal and three-dimensional echocardiography for segmental analysis and procedural guidance
Cardiac MRI for regurgitant volume and ventricular remodelling
Exercise echocardiography where symptoms and resting findings disagree
procedures: Surgical mitral repair — the preferred option in suitable degenerative disease
Mitral valve replacement with mechanical or bioprosthetic valves
Percutaneous mitral balloon commissurotomy for suitable rheumatic stenosis

keyPoints: Two leaflets: a deep anterior leaflet in fibrous continuity with the aortic valve, and a three-scalloped posterior leaflet.
Each papillary muscle supplies chordae to both leaflets, so a single papillary rupture affects the whole valve.
The posteromedial papillary muscle has a single coronary supply and is the one that ruptures after infarction.
Mitral closure produces the first heart sound.
Severe stenosis is generally defined by a valve area of about 1.5 cm² or less.

name: Pulmonary Valve
summary: A three-cusped semilunar valve between the right ventricular outflow tract and the pulmonary trunk, preventing regurgitation back into the right ventricle during diastole.

anatomy.location: The most superior and anterior of the cardiac valves, at the summit of the right ventricular infundibulum. Auscultated in the second left intercostal space at the sternal edge.
anatomy.shape: Three semilunar cusps — anterior, right and left — each with a lunule and a central nodule (nodule of Arantius). Behind each cusp the pulmonary trunk is slightly dilated, forming a sinus.
relations: Superiorly: the pulmonary trunk and its bifurcation
Posteriorly and to the right: the aortic root
Separated from the tricuspid valve by the supraventricular crest, so there is no fibrous continuity between them
attachments: Semilunar attachment to the wall of the right ventricular outflow tract and pulmonary trunk in a crown-like configuration
No chordae tendineae or papillary muscles
anatomy.bloodSupply: Small branches from the right coronary artery and the vasa vasorum of the pulmonary trunk; the cusps are essentially avascular.
anatomy.venousDrainage: Anterior cardiac veins and Thebesian veins of the right ventricular outflow tract.
anatomy.innervation: Cardiac plexus fibres reach the surrounding vessel wall rather than the cusps themselves.
anatomy.function: Opens when right ventricular pressure exceeds pulmonary arterial pressure, and closes when that gradient reverses at the end of systole.

physiology.function: Maintains forward flow into the pulmonary circulation and prevents diastolic backflow into the right ventricle. Closure produces the pulmonary component of the second heart sound.

pressures.label: Opening
pressures.value: RV pressure above pulmonary artery pressure — roughly 10–15 mmHg

physiology.electrical: Not electrically active, though the right ventricular outflow tract is a common origin of idiopathic ventricular tachycardia and ectopy.
hemodynamics: Pulmonary valve closure (P2) normally follows aortic closure (A2), and the interval widens on inspiration to produce physiological splitting of the second heart sound
Because right ventricular ejection is longer during inspiration, splitting is inspiratory
Chronic pulmonary regurgitation causes right ventricular volume overload — the dominant late problem after tetralogy of Fallot repair

pathology.name: Pulmonary stenosis
pathology.note: Usually congenital; produces right ventricular pressure overload and hypertrophy.

pathology.name: Pulmonary regurgitation
pathology.note: Commonly a long-term consequence of surgical repair of tetralogy of Fallot or balloon valvuloplasty; causes progressive right ventricular dilatation.

pathology.name: Carcinoid heart disease
pathology.note: Fibrous plaque deposition on right-sided valves causing mixed stenosis and regurgitation.

pathology.name: Infective endocarditis
pathology.note: Uncommon at this valve, but occurs with congenital lesions and indwelling devices.

clinical.relevance: Pulmonary valve disease is largely the territory of congenital and adult congenital cardiology, and transcatheter pulmonary valve implantation has substantially changed the management of the post-repair right ventricle.
conditions: Pulmonary regurgitation after tetralogy of Fallot repair
examination: Ejection systolic murmur in the second left intercostal space, louder on inspiration
Widely split second heart sound with a soft P2 in severe stenosis
Early diastolic Graham Steell murmur in pulmonary regurgitation with pulmonary hypertension
Right ventricular heave when the ventricle is pressure- or volume-loaded
imaging: Echocardiography for cusp morphology, peak gradient and regurgitation
Cardiac MRI for pulmonary regurgitant fraction and right ventricular volumes — the key data for timing intervention
CT for conduit anatomy and coronary proximity before transcatheter valve implantation
procedures: Balloon pulmonary valvuloplasty for congenital stenosis
Right ventricular outflow tract ablation for arrhythmia arising nearby

keyPoints: Three semilunar cusps; no chordae or papillary muscles.
The most superior and anterior cardiac valve, auscultated in the second left intercostal space.
Closure generates P2 — physiological splitting of S2 widens on inspiration.
Pulmonary stenosis is usually congenital rather than acquired.
Late pulmonary regurgitation after tetralogy of Fallot repair is a major cause of right ventricular dilatation.

name: Aortic Valve
summary: A three-cusped semilunar valve between the left ventricular outflow tract and the aorta. Two of its sinuses give rise to the coronary arteries.

anatomy.location: At the junction of the left ventricular outflow tract and the ascending aorta, occupying a central position within the heart with all other valves arranged around it. Auscultated in the second right intercostal space.
anatomy.shape: Three semilunar cusps — right coronary, left coronary and non-coronary — attached in a crown-shaped configuration. Behind each lies a sinus of Valsalva; the right and left sinuses give origin to the right and left coronary arteries respectively. A congenitally bicuspid valve occurs in roughly 1–2% of the population.
relations: Anteriorly and to the right: the right ventricular outflow tract
Posteriorly and to the left: the left atrium and the anterior mitral leaflet, in fibrous continuity
Inferiorly: the membranous interventricular septum and, immediately beneath it, the bundle of His
The valve sits at the centre of the cardiac fibrous skeleton
attachments: Crown-shaped semilunar attachment spanning the ventriculo-arterial junction
Aortomitral fibrous continuity with the anterior mitral leaflet
Membranous septum inferiorly, adjacent to the conduction system
No chordae tendineae or papillary muscles
anatomy.bloodSupply: The cusps are avascular and nourished by diffusion; the surrounding root receives vasa vasorum and small coronary branches.
anatomy.venousDrainage: Thebesian veins of the outflow tract and the vasa vasorum of the aortic root.
anatomy.innervation: Cardiac plexus fibres to the aortic root wall; cusps are essentially uninnervated.
anatomy.function: Opens when left ventricular pressure exceeds aortic pressure, and closes as ventricular pressure falls below it, producing the aortic component of the second heart sound and initiating diastolic coronary perfusion.

physiology.function: Directs the entire left ventricular stroke volume into the aorta and, on closing, sustains the aortic diastolic pressure that drives coronary flow.

pressures.label: Opening
pressures.value: LV pressure above aortic pressure — around 80 mmHg

pressures.label: Closure
pressures.value: at the dicrotic notch, generating A2

pressures.label: Severe stenosis
pressures.value: area under 1.0 cm², mean gradient of 40 mmHg or more, peak velocity of 4 m/s or more

physiology.electrical: Not electrically active, but the bundle of His runs immediately beneath the membranous septum — hence the risk of conduction block after surgical or transcatheter aortic valve replacement.
hemodynamics: Coronary flow occurs predominantly in diastole, sustained by the closed aortic valve and the elastic recoil of the aorta
Vortices within the sinuses of Valsalva help the cusps close smoothly and keep the coronary ostia patent
In stenosis, the pressure gradient is flow-dependent, so a low-output state can mask severe disease — the basis of low-flow, low-gradient aortic stenosis
In regurgitation, diastolic backflow widens the pulse pressure and reduces coronary perfusion pressure

pathology.name: Aortic stenosis
pathology.note: Calcific degenerative disease is the commonest cause in older adults; bicuspid morphology causes earlier presentation.

pathology.name: Aortic regurgitation
pathology.note: From cusp disease (bicuspid, rheumatic, endocarditis) or aortic root dilatation.

pathology.name: Bicuspid aortic valve
pathology.note: The commonest congenital cardiac malformation, associated with accelerated calcification and with aortopathy.

pathology.name: Infective endocarditis
pathology.note: May cause cusp destruction, root abscess and conduction disturbance.

pathology.name: Aortic dissection
pathology.note: Proximal dissection can disrupt cusp support and produce acute severe regurgitation.

clinical.relevance: Aortic stenosis is among the most common valve lesions requiring intervention, and the development of transcatheter aortic valve implantation has transformed treatment of older and higher-risk patients.
examination: Ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotids, with a slow-rising, low-volume pulse in severe stenosis
Soft or absent A2 and a narrow pulse pressure in severe stenosis
Early diastolic decrescendo murmur at the left sternal edge with a wide pulse pressure and collapsing pulse in regurgitation
The classic triad of angina, syncope and dyspnoea marking symptomatic severe stenosis
imaging: Transthoracic echocardiography for peak velocity, mean gradient, valve area and ventricular response
Dobutamine stress echocardiography in low-flow, low-gradient stenosis
Cardiac CT for calcium scoring, annular sizing and access planning before intervention
Cardiac MRI for regurgitant fraction and ventricular volumes
procedures: Surgical aortic valve replacement with mechanical or bioprosthetic valves
Aortic valve repair and valve-sparing root replacement in selected regurgitation
The Ross procedure in selected younger patients

keyPoints: Three cusps — right coronary, left coronary and non-coronary; the first two sinuses give rise to the coronary arteries.
Sits at the centre of the heart, in fibrous continuity with the anterior mitral leaflet.
The bundle of His lies just beneath it, explaining conduction block after valve intervention.
Closure produces A2 and sustains the diastolic pressure that drives coronary perfusion.
A bicuspid valve is the commonest congenital cardiac malformation, in roughly 1–2% of people.
